findings.case: Distance-dependent transmission reasoning after terminology help
findings.assessment: The student conflated placing bits onto the cable with their journey along it. Rather than treating that as a confirmed stable misconception, the generated diagnostic changed the transmission rate while holding distance and propagation speed constant, and asked for the ending event of each delay. This is a relevant probe of the proposed distinction, grounded in P07, P08, and P12, without supplying the answer.

findings.case: New correct observation after the generated diagnostic
findings.assessment: The next exact response correctly distinguished the sender finishing the last bit from a bit reaching the far end. The accepted evaluation changed the authorized controller state and the agent advanced, ending this session. Advancement was the only permitted tool at this point, so this proves evidence-sensitive progression, not an unconstrained choice among several instructional strategies.

findings.case: Instantaneous packet-entry reasoning without prior help
findings.assessment: The answer predicted the distance effect partly correctly but justified unchanged transmission using an explicit all-at-once packet-entry claim. Corrective feedback accurately distinguishes unchanged from zero transmission time and uses finite bit duration and Size/Bandwidth, grounded in P05, P07, and P08. Providing the answer here is appropriate post-assessment feedback. The existing controller queued a curated retest; the generated explanation was subsequently displayed in the actual student browser, but the retest remains unanswered.

educational_review.comparison: The two assessed misunderstandings produced educationally distinct diagnostic and explanation actions through controller-authorized choices. No instruction to alternate actions or satisfy action diversity was used in these cases. The permitted sets differed with accepted evidence and help history, so this is bounded adaptation within the existing controller, not proof of unrestricted model policy quality.
limits: The two terminology-help requests both selected alternative explanations, appropriately within the help-only clarify/explain set. They are not themselves evidence of adaptive assessment actions.

cautions: The upstream README sentence about derivative works conflicts with the CC BY 4.0 LICENSE adaptation grant. Both source files are retained; this package does not settle that legal inconsistency.
The source initially uses bandwidth/throughput loosely before distinguishing available rate from measured performance. Accept accurate explanations rather than penalizing synonyms alone.
The source uses latency generically. Every assessment specifies one-way latency or RTT explicitly.
The one-bit simplification in P08 is not assessed. Use finite packets and stated assumptions.

P10 contains a dimensional typo in the original displayed calculation: its denominator says 10 x 10^6 Mbps where 10 x 10^6 bits/s is intended. The 20-second result is correct. Preserve the source but use dimensionally correct arithmetic in assessment.
The source uses a simplified three-component delay model. Processing, multi-hop aggregation and advanced queuing models are outside assessment scope.
Queuing is introduced briefly. Questions use given waiting times, basic definition and delay arithmetic; traffic-dependent queue theory is not inferred from this excerpt.

approved_passages.text:
We often think of latency as having three components. First, there is
the speed-of-light propagation delay. This delay occurs because nothing,
including a bit on a wire, can travel faster than the speed of light. If
you know the distance between two points, you can calculate the
speed-of-light latency, although you have to be careful because light
travels across different media at different speeds: It travels at
3.0 × 10\ :sup:`8` m/s in a vacuum, 2.3 × 10\ :sup:`8` m/s
in a copper cable, and 2.0 × 10\ :sup:`8` m/s in an optical fiber.
Second, there is the amount of time it takes to transmit a unit of data.
This is a function of the network bandwidth and the size of the packet in
which the data is carried. Third, there may be queuing delays inside the
network, since packet switches generally need to store packets for some
time before forwarding them on an outbound link. So, we could define the
total latency as

::

   Latency = Propagation + Transmit + Queue
   Propagation =  Distance/SpeedOfLight
   Transmit = Size/Bandwidth

where ``Distance`` is the length of the wire over which the data will
travel, ``SpeedOfLight`` is the effective speed of light over that wire,
``Size`` is the size of the packet, and ``Bandwidth`` is the bandwidth
at which the packet is transmitted. Note that if the message contains
only one bit and we are talking about a single link (as opposed to a
whole network), then the ``Transmit`` and ``Queue`` terms are not
relevant, and latency corresponds to the propagation delay only.

Note that throughout this book we use the terms *latency* and *delay* in
a generic way to denote how long it takes to perform a particular
function, such as delivering a message or moving an object. When we are
referring to the specific amount of time it takes a signal to propagate
from one end of a link to another, we use the term *propagation delay*.
Also, we make it clear in the context of the discussion whether we are
referring to the one-way latency or the round-trip time.

content.text:
Your propagation-delay reasoning is correct: each bit travels twice as far at the same speed, so propagation delay doubles.

The part to revise is “the packet enters the cable all at once.” Picture the packet as a sequence of bit pulses, each occupying some time on the link. Transmission delay measures how long the sender takes to put that sequence onto the cable; propagation delay measures a signal’s travel along the cable.

Transmission delay = packet size / link rate. For a nonempty packet at a finite link rate, that takes time—it is not zero. Making the cable longer changes neither the packet size nor the link rate, so transmission delay stays unchanged.

We often think of latency as having three components. First, there is
the speed-of-light propagation delay. This delay occurs because nothing,
including a bit on a wire, can travel faster than the speed of light. If
you know the distance between two points, you can calculate the

travels across different media at different speeds: It travels at
3.0 × 10\ :sup:`8` m/s in a vacuum, 2.3 × 10\ :sup:`8` m/s
in a copper cable, and 2.0 × 10\ :sup:`8` m/s in an optical fiber.
Second, there is the amount of time it takes to transmit a unit of data.
This is a function of the network bandwidth and the size of the packet in
which the data is carried. Third, there may be queuing delays inside the
network, since packet switches generally need to store packets for some

total latency as

::

   Latency = Propagation + Transmit + Queue
   Propagation =  Distance/SpeedOfLight
   Transmit = Size/Bandwidth

where ``Distance`` is the length of the wire over which the data will
travel, ``SpeedOfLight`` is the effective speed of light over that wire,
``Size`` is the size of the packet, and ``Bandwidth`` is the bandwidth
at which the packet is transmitted. Note that if the message contains
only one bit and we are talking about a single link (as opposed to a
whole network), then the ``Transmit`` and ``Queue`` terms are not
relevant, and latency corresponds to the propagation delay only.

Note that throughout this book we use the terms *latency* and *delay* in
a generic way to denote how long it takes to perform a particular
function, such as delivering a message or moving an object. When we are
referring to the specific amount of time it takes a signal to propagate
from one end of a link to another, we use the term *propagation delay*.
Also, we make it clear in the context of the discussion whether we are
referring to the one-way latency or the round-trip time.

While you can talk about the bandwidth of the network as a whole,
sometimes you want to be more precise, focusing, for example, on the
bandwidth of a single physical link or of a logical process-to-process
channel. At the physical level, bandwidth is constantly improving, with
no end in sight. Intuitively, if you think of a second of time as a
distance you could measure with a ruler and bandwidth as how many bits
fit in that distance, then you can think of each bit as a pulse of some
width. For example, each bit on a 1-Mbps link is 1 μs wide, while each
bit on a 2-Mbps link is 0.5 μs wide, as illustrated in :numref:`Figure
%s <fig-bit-width>`. The more sophisticated the transmitting and receiving
technology, the narrower each bit can become and, thus, the higher the
bandwidth. For logical process-to-process channels, bandwidth is also
influenced by other factors, including how many times the software that
implements the channel has to handle, and possibly transform, each bit
of data.
